meta.title: Pharmy Case Study: One Searchable Clinical Trial Platform | Viesigners
meta.description: How Charles-Erick BG led the UX of one searchable clinical trial platform and tested a two-step form on real traffic.

sections.lead: With the project team, I led the UX and CRO of a clinical trial platform, from analysis to the winning version: *48% more visitors reached the form*, contact requests came from prequalified people, and the client got a data-driven roadmap.

sections.label: The friction
sections.h2: Two problems kept people *from joining a trial*

items.p: The client’s focus groups started this project. People were missing the information they needed to trust the platform and the process, and they needed a clinic close enough to reach.

items.h: A form that felt too long
items.p: My audit revealed friction in the qualification form, and people left before finishing it.
The client’s team received forms from unqualified people and lost time following up on them.
Each study had its own microsite, so the same general information was repeated on each one and harder to keep up to date.
One searchable platform for all the studies, instead of one microsite each:
list: Search by condition and location, like Airbnb for clinical trials
Easier updates for the client’s team

items.h: Test a new version on real traffic
items.p: From the client’s focus groups and my Google Analytics, Hotjar and form audit findings, we hypothesized that two changes would get more people to send their information, and qualify them first:
list: One study page merging the previous two, structured around the main objections, with just enough information to spark interest
A form split in two steps, to qualify people before they send their contact details

items.h: Split the form in two steps to receive only qualified forms
items.p: A *prescreener came first*, then contact details for people who qualified.

list.t: Two-step form (version B of the test).

notes.v: My audit showed people left the long form before finishing. A first step without personal details asks less up front and keeps people in the funnel.
The 2-step form required more build work, including a back button between the steps.

shots.label: Wireframe: form step 1 on mobile
shots.alt: Mobile wireframe of the first form step: a two-step stepper, eligibility questions and a See if you qualify button

items.h: Give people who don’t qualify a reason to stay
items.p: People who didn’t qualify could join a community through a *newsletter signup, placed on the thank-you screen* after the prescreener.

notes.v: The newsletter kept them in the loop, so the client could reach them again later and propose new trials better suited to them, without more effort from the client’s team.

items.h: Answer objections before asking people to search
items.p: A *strategic homepage sequence* answered objections and showed people they weren’t alone. Version B of the A/B test also *reduced the number of information pages*.

list: Land people directly on the map search.

list.t: Land people on a reassuring homepage before the search.

notes.v: Unanswered objections stop people from acting, as the focus groups showed. A search bar placed right under the top banner still sent people who were ready straight to the search.
Answering objections first added a step before the search.

items.h: Make distance visible with a map
items.p: People search by condition and location, and *see the clinics and trials on a map*.

notes.v: The focus groups showed people had to travel to the clinic, and acceptable distance varied by condition. A map search, inspired by Airbnb and real estate map apps, made that distance visible. One marker per condition would have been too cluttered, since a clinic could run several studies, so I grouped trials by clinic.
The map version was much harder to design and build. The developer and I worked together to use the map library’s built-in clustering options, which performed better and were simpler to implement.

sections.label: A design challenge that arose
prose: Merging the microsites into one platform meant two navigation systems on the same pages.

**I explored two options:** stacking the menus, or swapping to the microsite menu with a back button. Stacking adds cognitive load. Swapping is lighter, but “Back” means nothing to people who land directly on a microsite.

I stacked slim menus, with comfortable touch targets. On scroll, the platform menu slides away to free up space while the microsite menu stays; scrolling back to the top brings it back. On mobile, the hamburger menu handled the way back.

sections.label: What real users did
sections.h2: What the A/B test *showed, and what it didn’t*

reads.p: Version B got more people to check their eligibility, a narrowly significant result. And 47% of its submissions came from prequalified candidates.
The +20% isn’t significant on this sample, and version B changed the page and the form together. I flagged the sample size; the client chose to move forward.
Some prescreener fields caused friction, while qualified people filled in their contact details easily. On the not-qualified page, most people read the title and left.

stats.sub: A: content on two pages · B: content on one page
A: full form · B: prescreener only

items.h: A clear call on version B
items.p: I recommended keeping version B because it brought 48% more visitors to the form, and I was upfront about what the sample couldn’t confirm. That gave the client a decision it could trust.

I turned what people struggled with into a roadmap. They hit friction on prescreener fields, so I proposed simpler ones. Not-qualified visitors read the title and left, so I moved the community form to the top of a shorter page. I also proposed fewer calls to action on the study page.
I’d push for more traffic or a longer test. It ran for three months, but too few people reached the forms to confirm the submission result.

The contact step would be sent as soon as people moved to step 2, and the qualification questions would come in smaller chunks, so the form feels lighter. People who stopped after the contact step would receive an email sequence inviting them to finish, so the client’s team wouldn’t spend time on incomplete forms.
Right under the homepage banner, a section would show we understand people’s situation before talking about our solution (joining the trial participants community).
